title: AMD Shares Tumble 7% After Short Seller Questions China Ties. Chipmaker Denies Allegations.
detail:
AMD Shares Tumble 7% After Short Seller Questions China Ties. Chipmaker Denies Allegations.
Matias Civita
Thu, November 19, 2026 at 1:18 PM PST 3 min read
AMD
Trade AMD on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares of Advanced Micro Devices fell about 7% Wednesday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media published a report questioning the semiconductor company's business relationships in China and its exposure to U.S. export restrictions.

Hunterbrook, which said it had taken a short position in AMD, alleged the chipmaker faces significant regulatory risks tied to its commercial ties to Chinese companies. Among the report's allegations is that Chinese server manufacturer IEIT Systems continued receiving updated AMD firmware after being blacklisted by the U.S. government.

Firmware enables processors to operate within computer servers and other hardware systems. CNBC said it had not independently verified the allegations. AMD rejected the report's characterization of its operations, insisting that it complies with U.S. export regulations.

"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson told CNBC. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

Hunterbrook also alleged that AMD could face significant financial consequences if Washington introduces additional restrictions on semiconductor exports and business relationships involving China.

According to the investment firm's report, AMD bills more than 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong. Hunterbrook also claimed that the semiconductor manufacturer relies on a Chinese partner to complete production processes for most of its chips.

Those allegations raise questions about the company's exposure to potential changes in U.S. trade policy at a time when Washington is increasingly scrutinizing the semiconductor industry's commercial relationships with Beijing.

The report comes amid growing concerns surrounding rival Nvidia and investigations into its sales to Asian companies with ties to China. AMD had been viewed as a potential beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia, particularly as companies look for alternatives to the artificial intelligence chipmaker's products.

The United States has sought to restrict China's access to advanced American semiconductor technology over national security concerns, particularly regarding chips capable of supporting sophisticated artificial intelligence applications.

The restrictions have created challenges for American chipmakers seeking to maintain access to one of the world's largest technology markets without violating export regulations. Companies including AMD and Nvidia have previously explored developing products specifically designed to comply with U.S. restrictions while continuing to serve Chinese customers.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), a leader in AI accelerators, chips, and data-center networking hardware, closed at $145.98, down 3.30%. Strong third-quarter results, a raised outlook, and investor excitement over Anthropic's IPO supported shares early, but leadership and AI-spending concerns ultimately outweighed these factors. Wall Street is watching the next earnings cycle for AI-demand and supply insights.

Trading volume reached 311.8 million shares, coming in about 95% above its three-month average of 160.0 million shares. Nvidia IPO'd in 1999 and has grown 355,802% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) closed at 7,176, down 2.02%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) closed at 23,879, down 2.25%. Among semiconductor rivals, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) closed at $489.19, down 7.72%, and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) closed at $346.65, down 2.09%, underscoring pressure across semiconductors stocks.

What this means for investors

On Thursday, Nov. 19, Nvidia continued to face pressure even after strong Q3 results, as investors weighed artificial intelligence spending and leadership uncertainty. Nvidia's move shows Wall Street is still asking whether demand can justify the sector's pace of buildout.

Earlier this week, Morgan Stanley trimmed its price target to $260 while keeping an Overweight rating after the earnings release. That kept analyst attention on Nvidia's valuation and growth outlook.

On Nov. 17, Nvidia reported record fiscal Q3 revenue of $115.8 billion, representing 103% year-over-year growth, and said its new Vera Rubin NVL72 has shipped. Management also forecasted fiscal Q4 revenue of approximately $130 billion, ahead of Wall Street expectations. The Q3 update reinforced demand momentum in the AI sector.

Despite the spectacular results, the Nov. 12 resignation of Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang continued to weigh on shares, as investors are still recalibrating that risk alongside the earnings beat. Fallout from Huang's departure included the U.S. government tightening rules on Monday to prevent Chinese businesses from remotely accessing advanced Nvidia AI chips via overseas data centers.

This added to fears that incoming Democratic Congressional leadership will continue to add new regulations to the AI sector. As a result, AI stocks have been hit lately, despite the long-anticipated debut of Anthropic's IPO.

title: This Is Incredible News for AMD Stock Investors (Hint: It’s Bad News for Intel)

This Is Incredible News for AMD Stock Investors (Hint: It’s Bad News for Intel)
Harsh Chauhan, The Motley Fool

AMD
INTC
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) has been crushing Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) in the central processing unit (CPU) market, which explains why the former has been enjoying significantly stronger growth in recent quarters.

In fact, AMD is all set to become a bigger company than Intel in terms of revenue in the current quarter, and a closer look at the developments in the CPU market will tell us just why that's the case. Mercury Research, which provides data on the CPU market, recently released its third-quarter findings, which point to further gains for AMD in a lucrative space.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's take a closer look.

Image source: AMD.

AMD is becoming bigger in server CPUs

Server CPU demand has been increasing phenomenally owing to the growth in inference and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workloads in data centers. Counterpoint Research points out that the ratio of GPU (graphics processing unit) to CPU in AI data centers has moved from 4:1 to 2:1. What's more, the firm sees a GPU to CPU ratio of 1:1 amid rising demand for agentic AI.

In simpler terms, AI data centers are now using more CPUs per GPU, leading to a phenomenal increase in the total addressable market (TAM) for server CPUs. AMD predicts that server CPU TAM will hit $220 billion in 2030, clocking annual growth of more than 50% through the end of the decade. So, AMD's rising share in this space is good news for investors.

Mercury Research points out that AMD's server CPU market share increased to 35.5% in the third quarter, a significant improvement over the year-ago period's reading of 27.8%. So, Intel lost significant ground in this market, which explains why the growth of its data center and AI (DCAI) segment was much slower than AMD's in Q3.

While AMD posted a 97% year-over-year increase in data center revenue last quarter, Intel reported a 78% increase in this segment. The gap is poised to widen in the current quarter. That's because AMD is anticipating 66% revenue growth in the current quarter to $17 billion. Intel, on the other hand, expects 13% revenue growth in the current quarter to $15.5 billion, at the midpoint of its guidance range. That's slower than the 21% revenue jump Intel delivered in Q3.

AMD can continue hurting Intel in this market

It won't be surprising to see AMD taking more market share from Intel in server CPUs next year, thanks mainly to its sixth-generation server CPUs, codenamed Venice. All 20 tech stocks on a list from financial newsletter The Kobeissi Letter trade at least 25% below record highs. CoreWeave (CRWV) leads the slide at 76%.

Additionally, the S&P 500 has lost over $6 trillion in six weeks adding pressure to the markets in general. The Nasdaq Composite, however, sits in correction territory, a 10% decline, not the 20% that defines a bear market.

Why Are Cloud and Chip Names Falling Hardest?

The deepest drops cluster in cloud computing, chips, and data storage. Oracle (ORCL) and SanDisk (SNDK), a flash memory maker, each trail their highs by 68%. Nebius (NBIS), an artificial intelligence (AI) cloud provider, is down 66%.

Intel (INTC) is down 61%. Western Digital (WDC), a data storage maker, and Arm (ARM), a chip designer, each trail by 60%. Tesla (TSLA) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) show the mildest declines at 25%, still beyond the 20% bear market line.

CoreWeave, which rents computing capacity to AI developers, grew third-quarter revenue 168% to $3.66 billion. Its net loss still reached $709 million, with net interest expense at $846 million, according to its results.

A correction means a 10% decline from a record, while a bear market requires 20%. The Nasdaq Composite closed at 23,879.20 on Nov. 19. That sits below the 24,315.00 close that confirmed its correction on Nov. 5, CNBC reported.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 fell 2.02% on Nov. 19 to 7,175.83. AMD fell further after short seller Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a bet against the chipmaker.

Will the Indexes Follow These Tech Stocks Lower?

The Kobeissi Letter, meanwhile, has described the selloff as a historic opportunity. In both earlier 2026 episodes, in March and July, the Composite later set new records, a Motley Fool analysis shows.

If that pattern holds, indexes could recover while these 20 stocks lag. A close 20% below the Oct. 6 record, however, would most likely break it.

title: Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price
detail:
Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price
Jose Antonio Lanz

ANT
NVDA
AMD

Trading disclosure

Anthropic made stock market history Thursday, raising $81.34 billion in the largest initial IPO share sale ever. But Wall Street's response was considerably less enthusiastic than the demand for the Claude developer's shares.

The stock opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, a 34% premium over its $83 offering price, briefly pushing the company's fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion.

The rally faded quickly, however, with shares dropping toward $93 before closing today at $97.17.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The offering involved 980 million shares and surpassed SpaceX's original $75 billion IPO in June. As Decrypt previously reported, SpaceX's expanded final offering reached $86.25 billion, meaning Anthropic has not surpassed that completed deal.

Investors initially welcomed the listing, sending technology stocks higher before the opening bell. By the afternoon, however, the Nasdaq Composite was down 2.06%, the S&P 500 had fallen 1.9%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was off 2.17%.

AI stocks fall despite Anthropic's strong debut

The selloff extended across the AI supply chain. A Thursday afternoon market heatmap showed Nvidia falling 3.4%, Broadcom losing 2.07%, and memory chipmaker Micron slipping 2.17%. Microsoft was down 1.97%, while cloud infrastructure and software provider Oracle declined 2.97%.

AMD was among the hardest hit, down 7.73% in the day, although its decline had a separate catalyst. Reuters reported that the chipmaker came under pressure after investigative outlet Hunterbrook disclosed that its affiliated investment fund had taken a short position in the company.

The picture was not uniformly negative. Palo Alto Networks rose 6%, CrowdStrike gained 2.24%, and Intel added 2.25% in the same snapshot. The divergence shows that investors were distinguishing between companies rather than selling every technology stock indiscriminately.

The broader weakness comes as investors question the cost of building AI infrastructure and the returns companies can generate from that spending. Nvidia's latest earnings beat expectations, but uncertainty following Jensen Huang's resignation has continued to weigh on the semiconductor giant.

Anthropic also faces an expensive expansion. Its IPO disclosures detailed approximately $900.9 billion in infrastructure and computing commitments extending through 2045, alongside another $150 billion to $175 billion in estimated payments under less precisely defined arrangements.
